Shard writes plain Markdown files. Nothing is locked in — every note is a `.md` file you can back up, sync or open in another editor.

## Type / for anything

On an empty line, type `/` and the block palette opens at the cursor. Try `/table`, `/todo`, `/code` or `/callout`.

- [ ] Create a to-do like this one
- [x] Read this note

## Markdown shortcuts

Start a line with `# ` for a heading, `- ` for a bullet, `1. ` for a numbered list, `> ` for a quote, or ``` for code. The marker disappears as the block changes.

## Long-press to act

Long-press the handle at the left of a block to convert, move, duplicate or delete it. Long-press a table’s frame — or the strips above a column and left of a row — for its own controls. Menus open beside what they act on, never over the whole screen.

## Link your notes

Write [[double brackets]] to link a note, and #tags anywhere in the text. Backlinks appear at the bottom of every note, and the graph shows how everything connects.

> [!tip] Nothing to save
> Edits are written a moment after you stop typing. There is no save button.

Use this guide as a quick reference for files opened in Shard. Markdown (.md) uses a block editor; TeX (.tex) uses a raw LaTeX editor with a live preview and PDF export. Both formats remain plain text files in the vault.

A Markdown note is parsed into blocks when it opens and written back as ordinary Markdown when it saves. The focused block keeps its source markers visible; the reading view formats them and hides the markers.

# Heading → level 1 heading
## Heading → level 2 heading
### Heading → level 3 heading
**bold** → bold text
*italic* → italic text
~~deleted~~ → strikethrough
==highlight== → highlighted text
`code` → inline monospace code
- item → bulleted list
1. item → numbered list
- [ ] task → unchecked task
- [x] done → completed task
> quote → quote block
> [!warning] Attention → coloured callout
[label](https://example.com) → clickable web link
[[Note title]] → note link and backlinks
#tag → coloured tag and tag filter
![alt](image.png) → image block when it is on its own line
| A | B | → pipe table when followed by a separator row
```lang → fenced code block with optional language highlighting
--- → horizontal divider

Type a marker at the start of an empty line and press Space: #, ##, ###, -, *, +, 1., 1), [ ], [x], >. Typing ``` creates a code block; --- or *** creates a divider. Shard removes the trigger from the block and keeps the result as plain Markdown.

On an empty block, type / to open the command palette. Search by these names or their Ukrainian aliases:
/text → paragraph
/h1, /h2, /h3 → headings
/bullet → bulleted list
/numbered → numbered list
/todo → task with checkbox
/table → editable table
/code → fenced code block
/quote → quote
/callout → note/tip/warning callout
/divider → horizontal divider
/image → image block
/link → link to another note
/tag → tag
/date → today’s date

Tables, tasks, callouts, wiki links, tags and images are stored as Markdown, so they can be backed up or opened in another Markdown application. A task can also carry readable inline scheduling metadata: @priority(high), 📅 2030-04-05, @time(09:00), @remind(08:45) and @repeat(weekly). HTML and unsupported Markdown constructs are kept as raw paragraph text rather than silently deleted.

A TeX file opens in the raw source editor. Type a backslash to see command completion. The right pane is a fast visual approximation of the supported LaTeX subset; Export PDF uses the same parsed content and does not run a full TeX distribution.

\section{Title} → numbered section heading
\subsection{Title} → subsection heading
\textbf{bold} → bold text
\textit{italic}, \emph{italic} → italic text
\underline{text} → underlined text
\texttt{code}, \verb|code| → monospace text
$R \leq 1$ → inline math, for example R ≤ 1
\begin{equation} ... \end{equation} → centered numbered formula
\frac{a}{b} → fraction inside a formula
\begin{itemize} + \item → bulleted list
\begin{enumerate} + \item → numbered list
\begin{tabular}{...} → drawn table
\begin{figure} + tikzpicture → vector diagram and caption
\tableofcontents → generated table of contents
\label{key}, \ref{key} → cross-reference number
\pageref{key} → page reference marker
\cite{key} → numbered citation
\href{url}{label}, \url{url} → underlined link
\clearpage, \newpage → page break
\begin{landscape} ... → landscape page/table

\alpha → α \beta → β \gamma → γ \Delta → Δ
\to → → \leq → ≤ \geq → ≥ \neq → ≠
\approx → ≈ \equiv → ≡ \infty → ∞ \pm → ±
\times → × \cdot → · \int → ∫ \sum → ∑
\prod → ∏ \partial → ∂ \nabla → ∇ \in → ∈
\notin → ∉ \subseteq → ⊆ \forall → ∀ \exists → ∃
_{i} → ᵢ _{action} → ₐ𝚌ₜᵢₒₙ _{rec} → ᵣₑ𝚌

The preview understands the environments and commands listed above plus common spacing, list, bibliography and preamble commands. Commands such as \\usepackage, \\geometry, \\label and \\newcommand are used only to interpret the document or are hidden from the visual output. Unknown commands with a braced argument show the argument as text. Red underlines indicate unclosed braces, environments or math delimiters; fix them before exporting.
Tip: keep a small example note nearby while writing. The live preview is intentionally quick; the downloaded PDF is the canonical page-layout result.
